lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
In artisan gold mining, you cannot recover gold that is locked inside rock. Ore preparationâcrushing and millingâis the first step to liberate gold particles so they can be concentrated or amalgamated. If you skip or rush this stage, you leave gold in the tailings and waste your hard work. In many African artisanal operations, gold occurs as fine particles disseminated in quartz veins or as free flakes in alluvial gravel. Crushing reduces large rocks to small pieces; milling grinds them to powder, increasing surface area for chemical or physical extraction.

Consider this: a 10 kg rock with 5 grams of gold per tonne (5 g/t) contains only 0.05 grams of goldâabout the size of a grain of rice. If you crush poorly, that tiny grain may remain trapped in a big chunk and be discarded. Proper crushing and milling can recover over 90% of that gold, while poor preparation might recover less than 50%. That difference is your daily income.

In Africa, most artisanal miners use manual methods: hammers, pestles and mortars, or small jaw crushers. Mechanized mills like ball mills are common in larger operations. The goal is to reduce ore to a consistent sizeâtypically 100% passing a 2 mm sieve for gravity separation, or finer (75 microns) for cyanidation or amalgamation. The finer the grind, the more gold you expose, but over-grinding wastes energy and creates slimes that hinder recovery.

This module teaches you how to crush and mill ore safely and efficiently, using locally available tools. You will learn to select the right equipment, follow step-by-step methods, avoid common mistakes, and practice a complete ore preparation routine. Remember: good preparation is the foundation of profitable gold recovery.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To crush and mill ore effectively, you need the right tools. Start with safety gear: heavy leather gloves, safety glasses or goggles, a dust mask (N95 or better), and steel-toed boots. Dust from crushing contains silica, which causes silicosisâa deadly lung disease. Never work without a mask.

For manual crushing, you need a sledgehammer (4â6 kg) and a hardened steel plate or anvil. A flat granite or steel surface works well. For finer crushing, use a pestle and mortar made of hard wood or steel. In many African markets, you can buy a cast-iron mortar and pestle set for about $30â$50. For milling, a ball mill is ideal: a cylindrical steel drum that rotates with steel balls inside. Small ball mills (e.g., 1 m diameter, 1.5 m long) are available in mining supply shops in Ghana, Tanzania, and South Africa for $2,000â$5,000. Alternatively, a hammer mill or a stamp mill can be used. If mechanized options are too expensive, a manual grinding stone (like a metate) can grind small batches, but it is slow.

You also need screens or sieves. A set of sieves with mesh sizes 10 mm, 5 mm, 2 mm, and 1 mm helps control product size. A 200-mesh (75 micron) sieve is needed for fine milling. For transporting ore, use buckets, wheelbarrows, and shovels. A water source is essential for wet milling to reduce dust and improve grinding. Finally, a scale (at least 1 kg capacity) helps measure feed and product for consistency.

In rural areas, improvise: a car axle and a strong wooden frame can make a simple stamp mill. But always prioritize safety and efficiency. Invest in good toolsâthey pay back quickly in recovered gold.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Prepare the site. Choose a flat, stable area away from living quarters. Set up a crushing padâa large steel plate or concrete slab. Ensure good ventilation. Wear your safety gear.

Step 2: Sort and clean ore. Remove obvious waste rock, roots, and clay. Clay can be washed off with water. Sort ore by hardnessâharder rocks need more crushing.

Step 3: Primary crushing. Use a sledgehammer to break large rocks (up to 30 cm) into pieces smaller than 10 cm. Work on the steel plate. Aim for a pile of consistent size. This takes about 1 hour per 50 kg of ore for one person.

Step 4: Secondary crushing. Use a pestle and mortar or a smaller hammer to reduce pieces to less than 2 cm. You can also use a jaw crusher if available. Feed the crusher slowly to avoid jamming.

Step 5: Milling. If using a ball mill, fill it to 40â50% of its volume with ore and steel balls (typically 5â10 cm diameter). Add water to make a slurry (about 50% solids). Run the mill for 1â2 hours per 50 kg batch. Check grind size by taking a sample and sievingâaim for 80% passing 75 microns for amalgamation. If using a manual grinding stone, grind in small batches (1â2 kg) for 20â30 minutes until fine.

Step 6: Classification. After milling, pour the slurry through a series of screens to separate coarse particles. Return oversize to the mill for further grinding. The fine product goes to the next stage (e.g., sluice box, panning, or amalgamation).

Step 7: Clean up. Wash all equipment and the work area. Gold particles can stick to surfaces. Collect wash water and settle itâyou might recover fine gold. Record the weight of ore processed and the time taken to improve your efficiency.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Not crushing fine enough. Many miners stop at 2â3 cm pieces, leaving gold locked in coarse rock. Fix: Crush to at least 2 mm before milling. Use a sieve to checkâif 20% is oversize, crush more.

Mistake 2: Over-grinding. Grinding to dust (less than 50 microns) creates slimes that float and are hard to settle, causing gold loss. Fix: Monitor grind size. For gravity separation, 100â200 microns is ideal. For amalgamation, 75â100 microns. Stop when you reach target size.

Mistake 3: Using dirty equipment. Leftover material from previous batches can contaminate your ore. Fix: Clean hammers, mortars, and mills between batches. Use a brush and water. Do not mix different ore types without cleaning.

Mistake 4: Adding too much or too little water in ball mill. Too little water makes a paste that doesn't grind; too much water reduces impact forces. Fix: Aim for 50% solids by weight. A simple test: the slurry should flow like thick soup.

Mistake 5: Ignoring dust. Dry crushing creates silica dust that harms lungs. Fix: Always wear a mask. Wet the ore slightly before crushing if possible. Work upwind.

Mistake 6: Not checking mill ball charge. Worn or too few balls reduce grinding efficiency. Fix: Replace balls when they wear down to half their original size. Maintain ball charge at 40â50% of mill volume.

Mistake 7: Skipping classification. Sending coarse and fine particles together to concentration loses gold. Fix: Always screen after milling. Re-grind oversize.

Mistake 8: Poor record keeping. Without records, you cannot improve. Fix: Keep a log of ore weight, milling time, and gold recovered. Calculate recovery rate (gold recovered / gold in ore) to identify problems.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety in ore preparation is non-negotiable. The biggest hazard is silica dust. When you crush dry rock, fine dust fills the air. Inhaling it causes silicosis, an incurable lung disease. Always wear a NIOSH-approved N95 or P100 respirator. If you cannot afford one, at least use a wet cloth over your nose and mouthâbut this is not fully protective. Wet crushing reduces dust: sprinkle water on ore before hammering.

Hearing protection is also important. Hammering and ball mills are loud. Use earplugs or earmuffs. Eye protection prevents flying chips from injuring your eyes. Steel-toed boots protect your feet from falling rocks.

Ergonomics matter. Avoid lifting heavy rocks with your back. Use your legs. Take breaks every 30 minutes to stretch. Repetitive hammering can cause tendonitis. Alternate tasks.

Equipment safety: Before using a ball mill, check that all guards are in place. Never put your hands inside a running mill. Ensure electrical connections are safe and grounded. If using a diesel engine, keep it well-ventilated to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.

Best practices: Work in teams. Have a first aid kit with bandages, antiseptic, and eye wash. Know the location of the nearest clinic. Do not work alone. Keep children and animals away from the work area. Store tools safely.

Environmental best practices: Contain tailings to prevent erosion and water pollution. Do not dump mercury or chemicals into rivers. Use settling ponds for wash water. Reclaim land after mining.

Finally, maintain your equipment. A well-maintained hammer and mill last longer and work better. Lubricate mill bearings regularly. Replace worn parts. This reduces accidents and increases productivity.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Objective: Crush and mill a 20 kg sample of gold ore to 80% passing 75 microns, then evaluate your recovery potential.

Materials: 20 kg gold ore, sledgehammer, steel plate, pestle and mortar, ball mill (or grinding stone), set of sieves (10 mm, 5 mm, 2 mm, 1 mm, 200 mesh), water, buckets, scale, safety gear (gloves, goggles, mask, boots), notebook.

Procedure:
1. Weigh 20 kg of ore. Record weight.
2. Put on safety gear. Work in a well-ventilated area.
3. Primary crushing: Use sledgehammer to break ore to <10 cm. Time this step.
4. Secondary crushing: Use pestle and mortar to reduce to <2 cm. Time this step.
5. Milling: If using ball mill, add ore and water (50% solids) and run for 1 hour. If using grinding stone, grind in 2 kg batches for 20 minutes each. Time total milling.
6. Sieve analysis: Take a 500 g sample of milled product. Sieve through 2 mm, 1 mm, and 200 mesh. Weigh each fraction. Calculate percentage passing 200 mesh. Target: >80%.
7. If <80% passing, mill for another 30 minutes and re-test.
8. Once target reached, process the milled ore using your normal method (e.g., panning, sluice, amalgamation). Weigh gold recovered.
9. Calculate recovery: (gold recovered / gold in ore) x 100. Assume ore grade 5 g/t, so 20 kg contains 0.1 g gold. If you recover 0.08 g, recovery is 80%.

Analysis: Record all times, weights, and observations. Identify bottlenecks. Did crushing take too long? Was milling inefficient? Adjust your method next time.

Safety: Always wear mask during dry crushing. Wet ore before crushing to reduce dust. Do not overfill mill. Keep hands away from moving parts.

Extension: Repeat with different milling times (30, 60, 90 minutes) to find optimal time for your ore type. This exercise teaches you to optimize your own process.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Ore Preparation for Artisan Gold Mining

Ore preparation is the first and most consequential stage of any artisanal gold operation. Before a single gram of gold can be recovered, the host rock must be reduced from solid reef or alluvial gravel into a fine, liberated pulp. In the African artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) context â from the gold belts of Tanzania, Ghana, Zimbabwe, Burkina Faso, Mali, Kenya and Uganda â the efficiency of crushing and milling directly determines recovery rates, mercury consumption, operating cost and, ultimately, the margin per tonne. This practical reference consolidates the numbers, tools and checks you need to run ore preparation as a business, not just a chore.

Across Africa, ASM produces a significant share of national gold output. Ghana's ASM sector, for example, contributes a substantial portion of total gold production and employs over a million people directly and indirectly. Yet most operators lose 30â60% of recoverable gold at the crushing and milling stage because of poor size reduction, worn liners, or over-coarse grinding. Getting ore preparation right is the single highest-return intervention available to a small operator.

Why Size Reduction Governs Recovery

Gold in African ASM orebodies is usually fine-grained and locked inside quartz or sulphide matrix. Liberation â freeing the gold grains from the gangue â only happens when the ore is ground fine enough. If you stop at 5 mm, gravity tables and sluices will lose most of the fine gold. If you grind too fine, you create slimes that blind your recovery equipment and increase water and power costs. The practical target for most artisanal gravity circuits is a product size (P80) of 75â150 Âµm, roughly the fineness of fine flour.

Data Table 1 â Typical Crushing & Milling Stage Parameters

Stage Equipment Feed Size Product Size Typical Throughput (small plant)
Primary crushingJaw crusher200â400 mm50â100 mm2â10 t/h
Secondary crushingCone or hammer mill50â100 mm10â20 mm1â5 t/h
Fine grindingBall mill10â20 mm75â150 Âµm (P80)0.5â3 t/h
Gravity concentrationShaking table / sluice<2 mmConcentrate0.5â2 t/h

Source: Adapted from UNEP ASGM Toolkit (2022) and the U.S. Bureau of Mines Mineral Processing Handbook; throughput figures are indicative for African ASM operations and vary with ore hardness and equipment condition.

Data Table 2 â Cost & Performance Benchmarks (indicative, African ASM)

Item Unit Typical Range Business Impact
Jaw crusher (diesel)CapitalUSD 2,000â8,000Payback 3â12 months at 1â3 t/h
Ball mill (diesel/electric)CapitalUSD 3,000â15,000Determines liberation & recovery
Grinding media (steel balls)Consumable0.5â2 kg per tonne oreMajor operating cost driver
Diesel / electricityEnergy10â30 kWh per tonneUp to 40% of milling cost
Recovery improvement from correct grindYield+20â40% gold recoveryDirect revenue uplift

Source: Compiled from UNEP ASGM Toolkit (2022), World Bank State of the Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining Sector (2019), and field cost data reported in African ASM assessments (Ghana, Tanzania, Zimbabwe).

Step-by-Step Practical Method

  1. Characterise the ore. Take a 20â50 kg representative sample. Note hardness (quartz vs. soft oxide), moisture and visible sulphides. Hard quartz needs more grinding energy.
  2. Primary crush. Feed ROM ore to the jaw crusher. Keep the feed below the manufacturer's maximum to avoid jamming. Reduce to 50â100 mm.
  3. Secondary crush. Run through a cone or hammer mill to 10â20 mm. Remove tramp metal and wood to protect the mill.
  4. Grind. Charge the ball mill with ore, water and steel balls at the correct ball-to-ore ratio (typically 5:1 to 10:1). Run for the time determined by your grind test â usually 30â90 minutes per batch.
  5. Check the grind. Take a pulp sample, pan it, and feel for grit. If it feels sandy, grind longer. If it is slick slime, you have over-ground.
  6. Feed recovery. Send the pulp to your gravity circuit (shaking table, sluice, or centrifuge) or to leaching. Do not let pulp sit and settle â feed it promptly.
â  SAFETY WARNING â RESPIRATORY & MERCURY HAZARD

Crushing and milling generate fine silica dust that causes silicosis â an irreversible lung disease. Always wear a fitted dust mask (N95 or better), use water sprays or wet milling to suppress dust, and never dry-grind in an enclosed space without ventilation. If you use mercury downstream, know that grinding liberates more mercury-reactive gold and increases exposure risk. Mercury is neurotoxic â handle it only with gloves, in a ventilated area, and never burn amalgam indoors. Under the Minamata Convention, many African states now restrict mercury use in ASM.

Common Mistakes and Fixes

  • Under-grinding (coarse product). Fix: extend mill time or add a second grinding pass; test with a pan.
  • Over-grinding (slimes). Fix: shorten mill time, reduce ball charge, or add a classification step.
  • Wrong ball-to-ore ratio. Fix: weigh your charge; aim for 5:1 to 10:1 by mass.
  • Worn jaw plates or mill liners. Fix: inspect weekly; replace when clearance exceeds spec â worn liners cost recovery and energy.
  • Contamination. Fix: keep oil, grease and wood out of the mill; they coat gold and block amalgamation or leaching.
  • No representative sampling. Fix: sample every batch so you can calculate real grade and recovery.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Representative ore sample taken and hardness recorded.
  2. Jaw crusher feed size within manufacturer limit; no tramp metal.
  3. Secondary crusher producing 10â20 mm product.
  4. Ball mill charged at correct ball-to-ore ratio (5:1â10:1).
  5. Grind time verified by pan test â target P80 75â150 Âµm.
  6. Dust suppression (water spray or wet milling) active; masks worn.
  7. Worn liners and media inspected and replaced on schedule.
  8. Batch weight, grind time and recovery recorded for costing.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • UNEP â Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM) Programme & Toolkit
  • Minamata Convention on Mercury â Official Secretariat (ASM provisions)
  • U.S. Geological Survey â Mineral Processing & Gold Resources Publications
  • World Bank â Extractives & Artisanal Mining Knowledge
  • ILO â Safety and Health in Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of crushing and milling gold ore?
options: A) To increase the weight of the ore
B) To liberate gold particles from the rock matrix
C) To change the color of the ore
D) To make the ore easier to transport
quiz.explanation: Crushing and milling reduce rock size to expose gold particles for recovery.

quiz.q: Why is fine grinding important for gold recovery?
options: A) It makes the ore lighter
B) It increases surface area for chemical or physical extraction
C) It reduces the need for water
D) It makes the gold shiny
quiz.explanation: Finer particles expose more gold surface to extraction methods like amalgamation or cyanidation.

quiz.q: What is a typical target grind size for gravity separation?
quiz.explanation: Gravity methods like sluicing work best when ore is ground to 100â200 microns.

quiz.q: Which safety gear is most critical when dry crushing ore?
quiz.explanation: Silica dust causes silicosis, so a respirator is essential.

quiz.q: What is the recommended ball charge in a ball mill?
quiz.explanation: A 40â50% ball charge provides optimal grinding efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding water during ball milling?
options: A) To make the ore heavier
B) To reduce dust and improve grinding
quiz.explanation: Water suppresses dust and helps transport material through the mill.

quiz.q: Which sieve size is used to check for 75-micron grind?
quiz.explanation: 200 mesh corresponds to approximately 75 microns.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in ore preparation?
quiz.explanation: Many miners stop crushing too early, leaving gold locked in coarse rock.

quiz.q: How can you reduce silica dust during crushing?
options: B) Wet the ore before crushing
C) Work in an enclosed room
quiz.explanation: Wetting ore suppresses dust and reduces inhalation risk.

quiz.q: What is the ideal slurry density in a ball mill?
quiz.explanation: 50% solids by weight gives good grinding without being too thick or thin.

quiz.q: Why should you clean equipment between batches?
quiz.explanation: Leftover material can contaminate the next batch and skew recovery.

quiz.q: What is the consequence of over-grinding ore?
options: B) Creation of slimes that hinder recovery
quiz.explanation: Over-grinding produces slimes that float and are difficult to settle, causing gold loss.

quiz.q: How often should you replace worn mill balls?
options: B) When they wear to half their original size
quiz.explanation: Worn balls reduce grinding efficiency; replace when they are half size.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of classification after milling?
options: A) To separate coarse and fine particles
quiz.explanation: Classification ensures only fine particles go to concentration, while coarse particles are re-ground.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for ore preparation?
options: B) Keeping records of ore weight and recovery
quiz.explanation: Record keeping helps identify inefficiencies and improve recovery.

quiz.q: What is the recommended primary crushing size reduction?
quiz.explanation: Primary crushing breaks large rocks to about 10 cm using sledgehammers.

quiz.q: What tool is used for secondary crushing?
quiz.explanation: Pestle and mortar reduce 10 cm pieces to less than 2 cm.

quiz.q: How long should a ball mill run for a 50 kg batch?
quiz.explanation: 1â2 hours is typical to achieve a fine grind for 50 kg.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your mill is underloaded?
options: A) The mill makes a loud clanging noise
D) The slurry is too thin
quiz.explanation: A loud clanging noise indicates too few balls or too little ore, causing balls to hit the shell.

quiz.q: Why is it important to wear ear protection?
options: A) To hear the mill better
B) To prevent hearing loss from loud noise
quiz.explanation: Hammering and milling produce noise levels that can damage hearing.

quiz.q: What is the first step in ore preparation?
quiz.explanation: Removing waste and clay before crushing improves efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sieve set in ore preparation?
quiz.explanation: Sieves help ensure the ore is crushed and milled to the desired size.

quiz.q: Which of these is a health hazard from ore preparation?
quiz.explanation: Inhaling silica dust causes silicosis, a serious lung disease.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot afford a ball mill?
options: B) Use a manual grinding stone
quiz.explanation: A manual grinding stone can be used for small batches, though it is slow.

quiz.q: What is the recommended recovery target in the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: The exercise aims for at least 80% recovery to demonstrate good preparation.

quiz.q: Why should you record the weight of ore processed?
quiz.explanation: Knowing the feed weight allows you to calculate recovery and efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of ball mill jamming?
quiz.explanation: Feeding ore too quickly can overload the mill and cause jamming.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good practice for dust control?
options: A) Crushing dry ore in a closed room
D) Working on a windy day
quiz.explanation: Wetting ore reduces airborne dust significantly.

quiz.q: What is the ideal grind size for amalgamation?
quiz.explanation: Amalgamation requires fine particles (75â100 microns) for mercury to contact gold.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean the work area after milling?
options: A) To recover fine gold particles
quiz.explanation: Gold particles can stick to surfaces; cleaning and settling wash water recovers them.
